name: Decembrist revolt
info: The Decembrist revolt was a failed coup d’état by liberal officers and nobles of the Russian Empire, who rose in Saint Petersburg in December 1825 to replace the autocracy with a constitutional order and to end serfdom.

facts.where: the Russian Empire: Saint Petersburg, where the Northern Society met and the rising took place in Senate Square; Tulchin and Vasylkiv in Ukraine, centres of the Southern Society; Novohrad-Volynsky, where the Society of United Slavs was founded; afterwards places of exile across Siberia
facts.period: Union of Salvation from 1816; Union of Prosperity, suspended in 1821; Northern and Southern Societies 1821–1825; Society of United Slavs from 1823; the rising in Senate Square in December 1825; the Chernigov Regiment’s revolt in January 1826; trial and exile from 1826; amnesty 1856
facts.figures: Pavel Pestel, radical leader of the Southern Society; Nikita Muravyov, author of a constitution; Prince Sergei Trubetskoy, chosen as interim ruler, who deserted the rising; Prince Eugene Obolensky, who took his place; Sergey Muravyov-Apostol, leader of the revolt in Ukraine; Pyotr Kakhovsky; Maria Volkonskaya, who followed her husband into exile
facts.outcome: crushed by artillery in Saint Petersburg and in Ukraine; five leaders hanged and many others imprisoned or exiled to Siberia; the autocracy continued for almost a century, but the revolt has been considered the beginning of a revolutionary movement in Russia

t: Officers who had seen the Napoleonic Wars and the suffering of peasant soldiers formed secret societies from 1816, seeking a constitution and the end of serfdom.
In the confusion after Alexander I’s death in 1825 they led about 3,000 troops into Senate Square in Saint Petersburg, where loyal troops broke them with grapeshot at the end of the day.
Five leaders were hanged and many exiled to Siberia, where the Decembrists founded schools and brought new crops, and their wives’ devotion made the word Dekabristka a Russian symbol.
dyk: The rising failed partly because its chosen leader, Prince Sergei Trubetskoy, deserted it on the day, and his second-in-command, Colonel Bulatov, also vanished from the scene; the rebels had to appoint Prince Eugene Obolensky in a hurried consultation.
ev: Officers of the Imperial Russian Guard found the Union of Salvation, which takes a revolutionary turn when Pavel Pestel joins it
After a mutiny in the Semenovsky Regiment, the society suspends activity, but a Northern and a Southern Society carry on in secret
The Society of United Slavs is founded in Novohrad-Volynsky, seeking an equal federation of Slavic peoples
Alexander I dies suddenly, and parts of the army swear loyalty to Konstantin, unaware that he has renounced the throne
About 3,000 rebel troops refuse the oath to Nicholas I in Senate Square, Saint Petersburg, and are scattered by artillery
The Chernigov Regiment, led by Sergey Muravyov-Apostol, rises in Ukraine and is defeated within five days
The first party of Decembrist convicts sets out for Siberia, bound for the mines at Nerchinsk
On the accession of Alexander II the Decembrists are amnestied and their rights restored

sections.background:
Many officers were at first encouraged by the early liberal reforms of Tsar Alexander I, when liberalism was officially encouraged and expectations ran high. The chief advocate of reform was Count Mikhail Speransky, whose role grew greatly in 1808 and who drew up plans to reorganise Russia’s government until 1812, when hostility forced him into exile. In 1818 the tsar asked Count Nikolay Novosiltsev to draw up a constitution, and serfdom was abolished in the Baltic provinces between 1816 and 1819. But unrest at home and abroad, which the tsar blamed on political liberalisation, led to a series of repressions and a return to conservatism.

Meanwhile the experience of the Napoleonic Wars and the suffering of peasant soldiers drew officers and their sympathisers to the cause of reform. They showed their contempt for the court by rejecting its way of life, wearing their cavalry swords at balls to show that they would not dance, and devoting themselves to study, embracing both the peasants and the reform movements of intellectuals abroad. Historians have noted that the American Revolution and the United States Declaration of Independence may also have influenced them.

The crisis that gave them their chance came with the succession. Alexander’s brother and heir, Grand Duke Konstantin Pavlovich, had privately renounced the throne two years before Alexander’s sudden death on 1 December 1825, leaving the crown to their younger brother Nicholas. Neither the government nor the public knew of the renunciation, and parts of the army swore loyalty to Konstantin.
sections.aims:
The Decembrists wanted to replace the autocracy of the Russian Empire with a constitutional order, and from the beginning they considered freeing the serfs. Pavel Pestel wrote that they first hoped to have a majority of the nobility petition the emperor for it, but soon realised that the nobility could not be persuaded. The constitution written by Nikita Muravyov was highly similar to the United States Constitution, though the Decembrists opposed slavery in the United States.

The two main societies differed. The more moderate Northern Society sought a British-style constitutional monarchy with a limited franchise and a legislative assembly, which might become a republic in future only by the will of the people. It did not call for the execution of the imperial family, and it supported equality before the law and the abolition of serfdom with the land kept by the landlords, as in the Baltic provinces. The Southern Society, under Pestel’s influence, was more radical: it wanted to abolish the monarchy, establish a republic and redistribute the land, taking half into state ownership and dividing the rest among the peasants.

The Society of United Slavs had a similar programme but laid its main emphasis on a future equal federation of Russia, Poland and the other Slavic and Vlach lands. Many Decembrists, by contrast, wanted classical liberalism or a moderate conservatism rather than Pestel’s more Jacobin, centralising programme.
sections.events:
In 1816 officers of the Imperial Russian Guard founded the Union of Salvation, which took a revolutionary cast when Pavel Pestel joined it. It gave way to the Union of Prosperity, which had no revolutionary plans, and after a mutiny in the Semenovsky Regiment in 1820 the society suspended activity in 1821. Two groups carried on in secret: a Southern Society at Tulchin in Ukraine, led by Pestel, and a Northern Society in Saint Petersburg. In September 1825 the Society of United Slavs joined the Southern Society.

When Konstantin’s renunciation became public and Nicholas stepped forward, the Northern Society tried in secret meetings to persuade regimental leaders not to swear allegiance to him. On the morning of 26 December 1825 (14 December in the Old Style calendar) officers commanding about 3,000 men assembled in Senate Square, refused the oath to Nicholas I and proclaimed their loyalty to Konstantin. The rest of the garrison did not join them, and their leader, Prince Sergei Trubetskoy, deserted. For hours they faced 9,000 loyal troops before a vast crowd. Count Mikhail Miloradovich, sent by Nicholas to parley, was fatally shot by Pyotr Kakhovsky. After a cavalry charge failed on the icy cobbles, Nicholas at last had three guns fire grapeshot; rebels fleeing across the frozen Neva were shelled, and many sank as the ice broke.

In the south Pestel had been arrested the day before. On 10 January 1826 the Chernigov Regiment, led by Sergey Muravyov-Apostol, rose and captured Vasylkiv, but it was defeated within five days and over 3,000 people were arrested.
sections.people:
The Decembrists were liberal military and political dissidents, many of them nobles and guard officers; the Southern Society was dominated by army officers and landowners from Left-bank and Southern Ukraine, Sloboda Ukraine and Volhynia. Pavel Pestel was the outstanding figure of the Southern Society, and Yakushkin, who wished to kill the emperor even before a revolution, left the Union of Salvation when the others refused. The Northern Society was led by the guard officers Nikita Muravyov, Prince Sergei Trubetskoy and Prince Eugene Obolensky. Trubetskoy was elected interim ruler but deserted the rising, and Obolensky replaced him on the day. Sergey Muravyov-Apostol, freed by force by the United Slavs after his arrest, led the revolt in Ukraine.

Not all who took part shared the same fate. Ordinary soldiers, the “soldier-Decembrists”, felt the emperor’s vengeance in full: sentenced by court-martial, many received thousands of lashes and walked to Siberia chained alongside criminals. Of the exiled officers, Dimitri Zavalishin later helped shape Russian policy in the Far East.

The wives of many Decembrists, and some sisters and nieces, gave up privilege and comfort to follow them into exile. Under the leadership of Princess Maria Volkonskaya, the wife of Sergei Volkonsky, they petitioned without rest and by 1832 had won the formal cancellation of their husbands’ labour and the right to live with them in privacy. The word Dekabristka, “Decembrist wife”, became a Russian symbol of a wife’s devotion.
sections.outcomes:
The revolt failed. Disorganised by indecision and dissension among its leaders, the rebels in the capital waited in vain for the rest of the troops, and the rising in Ukraine faced superior forces armed with artillery. A court tried 61 people of the Northern Society, 37 of the Southern Society and 23 of the United Slavs. Five leaders were hanged, and many other participants were imprisoned or exiled to Siberia. About 120 members of the secret societies were punished without trial, by imprisonment in a fortress, demotion or transfer to the army in the Caucasus; of the soldiers, 178 were sentenced to run the gauntlet, and about four thousand were formed into a combined guards regiment and sent to the Caucasus.

The first party of convicts left for Siberia on 25 July 1826. The largest group was held at Chita and moved three years later to Petrovsky Zavod, near Nerchinsk; most left between 1835 and 1837 to settle in Siberian towns, under police watch and with every letter censored. On 26 August 1856, on the accession of Alexander II, the Decembrists were amnestied and their rights restored, though many chose to stay in Siberia.

With their failure Russia’s autocracy continued for almost a century; serfdom was abolished only in 1861 and parliaments were established in 1905. Yet their dissatisfaction forced Nicholas I to turn to the empire’s problems, and in 1826 he put Speransky at the head of a committee to codify Russian law, which produced a collection of 35,993 enactments.
sections.legacy:
In exile the Decembrists deeply influenced Siberian life. At Petrovsky Zavod they taught each other languages, crafts and music and set up “academies” of libraries, schools and symposia. In their settlements they founded many schools for native people, the first at Nerchinsk, and schools for women; they introduced crops such as vegetables, tobacco, rye, buckwheat and barley and methods such as hothouse growing, and their doctors organised medical aid. Their exile planted a lasting intelligentsia in Siberia, for the first time a cultural and political elite living there permanently.

To some extent the Decembrists stood in the tradition of the palace revolutionaries of 1725–1825, who wanted to put their own candidate on the throne, but unlike earlier Romanov palace revolutions their rising has been considered the beginning of a revolutionary movement: it was the first open breach between the government and the reformist nobility, which would widen. Their call for reform, including the end of serfdom, made them idols of the populist movement of the 1860s and 1870s.

Though the subject was proscribed under Nicholas I, Alexander Herzen put the profiles of the executed Decembrists on the cover of his periodical Polar Star. Alexander Pushkin addressed poems to Decembrist friends, Nikolai Nekrasov wrote a long poem about their wives, and Leo Tolstoy began a novel about them that grew into War and Peace. Yuri Shaporin’s opera The Decembrists premiered at the Bolshoi Theatre in 1953, and the revolt is portrayed in the 2019 Russian film Union of Salvation.

summary: The Decembrist revolt was the failed rising of liberal officers and nobles in Saint Petersburg in December 1825, after secret societies formed from 1816 had sought a constitution and the end of serfdom. Artillery scattered the rebels, five leaders were hanged and many were exiled to Siberia, but the revolt has been seen as the beginning of Russia’s revolutionary movement.

Dates: start 1816 (Union of Salvation) and end 1826 (the Chernigov Regiment’s revolt of January 1826 and the trial and exile). The rising itself is 1825; the amnesty of 1856 is given as an event only.

Calendar: the article gives Gregorian dates with the Old Style in brackets (26 December [O.S. 14 December] 1825; Alexander’s death 1 December [O.S. 19 November]; Pestel arrested 25 December [O.S. 13 December]; Chernigov rising 10 January 1826 (O.S. 29 December 1825)). I used the Gregorian dates in the text, giving the Old Style once for Senate Square.

Sentences: the lede says “five rebellion leaders were sentenced to hanging”; the trial section lists “to death - five by quartering, 31 - by beheading” and says the court meant to apply no punishment but hanging. I wrote only that five leaders were hanged.
Numbers: 61 + 37 + 23 = 121 tried, but the Siberia section speaks of “Fifteen out of 124 Decembrists”. I used the 61/37/23 figures only.

The article uses both “Union of Prosperity” and “Union of Welfare” for what seems to be the same society; I used Union of Prosperity. It also spells Muravyov, Muraviev and Murav’yov, Trubetskoy and Trubetskoi, Eugene and Yevgeny Obolensky; I used Nikita Muravyov, Sergey Muravyov-Apostol, Sergei Trubetskoy and Eugene Obolensky.
The town captured by Muravyov-Apostol is “Vasilkov” in one place and “Vasylkiv council” in another; I wrote Vasylkiv.
Left out the Polish patriotic society’s aims and the long list of lands of the United Slavs’ federation for length; the rumour of bodies thrown into the Neva is not used.
